notes:
I covered most verses, but there are gaps. My searches turned up nothing on vv. 34, 39–41 or 45–46, so I've left them out. I also found nothing from Lutheran, Pentecostal, Anglican or Orthodox teachers, nothing from bibleodyssey.org or the netbible.org notes, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this passage. The main Enduring Word page was cut off before vv. 25–47, so most of its notes come from search snippets. Some of those snippets are marked on the page as an AI-written summary. I've flagged that where it matters.

---

**v. 25**
- Matthew Henry: The exercising of lordship better becomes the kings of the Gentiles than the ministers of Christ. Leaders in the church who chase outward pomp and power cheapen their office. He compares it to Israel asking for a king like the nations around them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm
- Henry also sees the disciples' quarrel as a sad sign of later fights over supremacy in the churches. Same URL.

**v. 26**
- Catholic reading (catholic.com): strengthening the brethren in v. 32 is exactly the kind of leadership described here, being "greatest" by being "youngest." On this reading Peter, made servant of all, is to be the leader among the apostles. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-one-who-serves

**v. 27**
- Henry: Christ was among his disciples just like one that waited at table. He points to Jesus washing their feet. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm

**v. 28**
- Henry: the disciples could give Jesus little real help, and they had many faults. Yet he passes over these and praises them for staying with Him, though they stayed only because of His own grace. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm

**vv. 29–30**
- Henry: this kingdom was given to the apostles and to those after them in gospel ministry. They "sit on thrones" as officers of the church: they pronounce judgment on unbelieving Israel and govern the spiritual Israel through church discipline. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm
- Protestant–Catholic debate: the catholic.com article quotes James White, a Reformed Baptist writer. White argues Jesus "treats all the disciples alike and speaks of conferring on them all—not on Peter alone—a kingdom". The Catholic author replies that the following verses single Peter out. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-one-who-serves

**v. 31**
- David Guzik (Enduring Word): Jesus knew of a spiritual battle going on behind the scenes. Satan wanted to crush Peter completely. Guzik quotes Geldenhuys: Satan wants none of the wheat to remain, so that all are blown away like chaff, as Judas was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Henry: Satan could not sift them without God's permission, just as he asked leave to test Job. Henry also mentions a view that the sifting was punishment for their quarrel over who was greatest. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm
- Catholic reading: in the Greek, "you" in v. 31 is plural (all the apostles), but in v. 32 it is singular (Peter). https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-one-who-serves

**v. 32** (the main point where traditions differ)
- Guzik: Peter wasn't completely crushed, and that had nothing to do with Peter himself. It was because Jesus prayed for him. The page's AI summary draws the lesson that our protection rests on Jesus' prayers for us, not on our own strength. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Spurgeon (Baptist): if Jesus prays for His people, He will surely be heard. He will lift Peter out of Satan's sifting, and the task "strengthen thy brethren" shows He expects to. Spurgeon applies it to restored believers helping to recover others. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/peter-after-his-restoration/
- Desiring God (Baptist): sets Peter beside Judas. Later, rather than both betraying Jesus, we see Peter strengthening his brothers to replace Judas, the traitor who did not turn. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/when-jesus-prays-for-your-faith
- Henry: those who fall must turn back, and once restored must help keep others from falling. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm
- Catholic reading: in front of the other apostles, Jesus prays for Peter alone and gives him alone the role of strengthening them. The article reads this as Peter's primacy. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-one-who-serves

**v. 33**
- Henry: every true disciple sincerely wants to follow Christ wherever He leads, even to prison or out of the world. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm

**vv. 35–36** (the sword: a real disagreement)
- Henry: the disciples must now expect trouble and suffer like their Master. The sword saying only shows how dangerous the times would be. But the sword of the Spirit is the sword which the disciples of Christ must furnish themselves with. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm
- Calvin (Reformed): Jesus isn't calling them to outward fighting. He uses fighting as a picture of the hard spiritual struggles and temptations ahead. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-36.html
- Wesley (Methodist): clearly not meant literally; it only means a time of extreme danger is coming. Same URL.
- Gill (Baptist): not literal. Two swords could never be "enough" for eleven men, and Jesus soon forbade Peter to use one. Same URL.
- Barnes (Presbyterian): the instructions concern the disciples' future life, not the arrest, since there was no time to buy swords that night. He concludes that self-defence is lawful, but that this doesn't prove offensive war is lawful. Same URL.
- Constable (dispensational evangelical): the purse, bag and sword are probably metaphors for being personally prepared, including relying on God and His Word. He notes Jesus later rebuked Peter for using a sword. Same URL.
- Ellicott: the mention of the sword adds something new. Jesus' words to Peter in Matthew 26:52 show the sword was not meant for His defence. https://biblehub.com/luke/22-36.htm
- J. Vernon McGee (popular radio teacher) reads it literally as approving self-protection. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-36.html
- Catholic: one catholic.com piece says that here Jesus approves of taking up a sword for self-defense. Forbidding the sword in one situation doesn't forbid all defence. https://www.catholic.com/audio/scw/year-a-seventh-sunday-of-ordinary-time

**v. 37**
- One explanation: carrying weapons would make the group look like lawbreakers. That fits Isaiah 53:12, Jesus "numbered with the transgressors." https://biblehub.com/q/Interpret_buy_a_sword_in_Luke_22_36.htm
- Another Bible Hub article: Jesus' group might look criminal or seditious to the authorities, even though it wasn't. https://biblehub.com/q/why_did_jesus_tell_them_to_buy_swords.htm

**v. 38**
- Clarke: "It is enough" can't mean two swords were sufficient, since nine disciples would have none. He takes it as pointing to Peter's (and perhaps others') readiness to defend Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-38.html
- Benson: the disciples misunderstood what He meant about swords. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-36.html
- A Bible Hub article: "It is enough" is an idiom that closes the conversation. It doesn't mean two swords were militarily adequate. https://biblehub.com/q/Is_Luke_22_36_a_call_for_Christian_defense.htm

**v. 42**
- Guzik: the cup stood for judgment, not death. Jesus drank the cup of the Father's fury so we would not have to, and this was the source of His greatest agony. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/

**v. 43**
- Henry: it shows how deeply Jesus humbled Himself that He needed and accepted an angel's help. The angel probably encouraged Him with the joy set before Him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm
- Manuscript question: Utley names vv. 43–44 as one of the chapter's two great textual difficulties. He lists manuscripts that include the verses and early writers who quote them (Justin Martyr, Irenaeus and others). https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-22
- A Bible Hub article argues the verses are original. It says some copies may have dropped them because they troubled early scribes, since some 2nd-century groups denied Jesus was truly human, or by a copying slip. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_Luke_22_43_missing_in_some_texts.htm

**v. 44**
- Ellicott: the Greek word for "agony" mainly means a struggle or conflict, not just physical pain. He thinks the verses were left out of many old manuscripts out of "mistaken reverence," and notes Athanasius condemned anyone who denied the bloody sweat. https://biblehub.com/luke/22-44.htm
- Gill: only Luke records it, perhaps because he was a physician. He says the verses are missing from some copies, as Jerome and Hilary noted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/22-44.htm
- Henry: the sweat came on a cold night in the open air, which shows how extreme His anguish was. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm
- A medical explanation: Wiersbe, cited in the Light of Israel commentary, suggests hematidrosis, where great stress makes tiny blood vessels in the sweat glands burst. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/22-43.html

**v. 47**
- Guzik: the size of the crowd shows the leaders saw the arrest as dangerous. He quotes a source saying Roman soldiers were part of the crowd (John 18:3, 12). Judas, kissing while betraying, is an example of a seared conscience. Judas bears full responsibility, yet God used the betrayal to deliver Jesus to His enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-22/
- Henry: nothing grieves Christ more than being betrayed with a kiss by people who claim to belong to Him and love Him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_022.cfm
